thoughts: ㄱ is the Korean plain velar stop. For English speakers it maps roughly to K/G, but the key differences are (1) it’s usually unaspirated (little to no puff of air) and (2) as a final consonant it’s an unreleased stop.
description: Pronounce ㄱ with the back of your tongue against the soft palate (like English K/G). At the start of a syllable it sounds like a soft, unaspirated “k” (closer to the k in “skate” than the strongly puffed k in “kite”). Between vowels it often sounds more like a gentle “g”. At the end of a syllable (batchim) it becomes an unreleased [k̚]: stop the sound abruptly without releasing a final “k” puff.

thoughts: ㄲ is the Korean “tense” (fortis) version of ㄱ. It’s pronounced with strong muscular tension and almost no aspiration (no noticeable puff of air). In final position (batchim), ㄲ is not released and sounds like a clipped, unreleased K, the same way ㄱ/ㅋ are neutralized at the end.
description: Pronounce ㄲ as a very tight, hard “k” sound with **little to no air**. It can feel like the **k in ‘ski’** (unaspirated) but **stronger and tenser**. Don’t let it turn into an English “g” (voiced), and don’t add a big puff of air like the “k” in ‘kite’ (that would be ㅋ). When ㄲ is a final consonant (batchim), it becomes a **short, unreleased [k̚]**—like saying ‘back’ but stopping before you release the final k.

thoughts: ㄴ is the Korean “n” sound (an alveolar nasal), very close to English. The main thing to watch is that in the ㄴ+ㄹ (or ㄹ+ㄴ) environment it turns into a long L sound [ll]. Also, syllable-final ㄴ is held briefly with no extra vowel after it.
description: Pronounce ㄴ like the English “n” in “no,” with the tongue touching the ridge just behind your upper front teeth. At the end of a syllable (받침), keep it short and clean—don’t add an extra “uh” after it. Special case: when ㄴ is next to ㄹ (ㄴㄹ or ㄹㄴ), it’s normally pronounced as a long “L” sound (both become [ll]), similar to a doubled L.

In some contexts (often after another consonant), ㄷ may be heard as a **tense, tight ‘tt’**.

thoughts: ㄹ is the famous Korean “R/L” sound. It’s not the English R: it’s usually a quick tongue tap (like a soft Spanish r or the American English quick ‘tt’ in “butter”), but it becomes an L sound at the end of a syllable or before another consonant. English speakers often over-pronounce it as a strong English R or a very dark L.
description:
Pronounce ㄹ in two main ways depending on position:
- Between vowels or at the start of a syllable: a quick tap [ɾ], similar to the single r in Spanish “pero” or the quick ‘tt’ sound many Americans use in “butter.” Don’t curl your tongue like an English R.
- At the end of a syllable (before a consonant or word-final): an L-like sound [l]. Keep it relatively “light” (tongue on the ridge behind the upper teeth), not as dark/velarized as many English final L’s.
Also, ㄴ + ㄹ often becomes a long L sound (effectively [ll]) in pronunciation.

thoughts: ㅂ is the Korean “plain” bilabial stop. To English ears it can sound like a soft P at the start of a syllable, more like B between vowels, and like an unreleased P at the end. The main trap for English speakers is adding too much aspiration (a strong puff of air) like English P.
description:
Pronounce ㅂ with both lips closing (like English P/B), but **with little to no puff of air**. 
- **At the beginning of a syllable**: sounds between English **P** and **B** (often like the P in *spin*, not the strongly aspirated P in *pin*).
- **Between vowels**: often sounds more **B-like** (voiced).
- **At the end (받침)**: becomes an **unreleased [p̚]**—close the lips to stop the sound, but don’t release a burst.
- **Before ㄴ/ㅁ**: commonly **assimilates to [m]** in natural speech (ㅂ → ㅁ before a nasal).

thoughts: ㄳ is a final-consonant cluster (받침) made of ㄱ+ㅅ. In most positions it simplifies to a single ㄱ sound, but if the next syllable starts with a vowel the ㅅ links over and usually becomes tense ㅆ. It can also nasalize to ㅇ before ㄴ/ㅁ, just like a normal final ㄱ would.
description:
How it sounds:
- At the end of a syllable (or before another consonant), ㄳ is pronounced like a final ㄱ: an unreleased “k” sound [k̚], similar to the end of English “back,” but with less audible release.
- Before a vowel (when the next syllable starts with ㅇ+vowel), the ㅅ moves to the next syllable and is usually pronounced as tense ㅆ [s͈]. So it often sounds like “k-ss…” (e.g., 몫이 ≈ “mok-ssi”).
- Before ㄴ or ㅁ, that final ㄱ often nasalizes to ㅇ [ŋ] (like “ng”) (e.g., 몫만 ≈ “mong-man”).

If a consonant follows, you still hear “n”, but the next consonant often becomes tense: 앉다 → 안따, 앉고 → 안꼬.

thoughts: ㄶ is a 받침 (final-consonant) combination: you usually hear an /n/ sound, while the ㅎ is often silent but changes the next sound (most importantly by aspirating it). The tricky part for English speakers is applying the linking/aspiration rules automatically in running speech.
description:
Pronounce ㄶ basically as an “n” sound in the syllable-final (batchim) position. The ㅎ is usually not pronounced as a clear English “h,” but it often affects the next syllable:
- Before a vowel (next syllable starts with ㅇ): the ㅎ drops, and the ㄴ links over → sounds like -나-, -니-, etc. (e.g., 많아 ≈ 마나).
- Before a consonant like ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅈ/ㅂ: the ㅎ makes the next consonant aspirated (ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅊ/ㅍ) while the 받침 is still heard as ㄴ (e.g., 많다 ≈ 만타).
- At the end of a word: you typically just hear ㄴ (많 [만]).

description:
How it’s pronounced:
- At the end of a syllable (or before another consonant), ㄻ is usually simplified to just ㅁ [m]. The ㄹ is not heard. Example idea: 삶 sounds like “sam”.

Tip: Don’t try to force an English-style consonant cluster at the end of one syllable; either end it as an “m”, or (before a vowel) think of it as starting the next syllable with an “l”.

thoughts: Pattern ㄼ is a complex final consonant (batchim) made of ㄹ+ㅂ. English speakers know the individual sounds (L/B/P), but the Korean rule-based alternations (often sounding like just ㄹ, sometimes just ㅂ, and sometimes splitting across syllables before a vowel) are usually unfamiliar.

If the next syllable starts with a vowel (i.e., ㅇ + vowel), it often “splits”: ㄹ stays as the coda and ㅂ moves to the next syllable as a starting consonant, sounding like “-lb-” (e.g., 덟이 → [덜비]). description:
Pronunciation depends on what comes next:
- Before a pause or a consonant: ㄽ is pronounced as ㄹ only (the ㅅ is not heard). Think of a clean Korean L held at the end of the syllable.
- Before a vowel (next syllable starts with ㅇ): the ㄹ stays as the final L, and the ㅅ moves to the next syllable as its onset (so you hear an L + s sound). If the next vowel is ㅣ (or sounds like ㅣ), that ㅅ will sound more like English “sh” (the normal Korean ㅅ-before-ㅣ effect).
Tip: don’t try to pronounce a tight English-style “l+s” cluster inside one syllable; in Korean it splits across the syllable boundary.

description:
How it sounds depends on what comes next:
- **Before a pause or before another consonant:** ㄾ is pronounced mostly as a final **ㄹ [l]** (like the “l” in *fall*, but with a shorter, cleaner stop). The **ㅌ** isn’t clearly released.
- **Before a vowel (next syllable starts with a vowel):** the **ㅌ moves to the next syllable**, so you hear **…l-t…** (an aspirated Korean **t**, with a noticeable puff of air).
- **Before certain consonants (like ㄷ, ㄱ, ㅂ, ㅅ, ㅈ):** the hidden **ㅌ** often causes **tensing** of the next consonant (e.g., ㄷ → ㄸ), so it can sound like **…l-tt…**.

Tip: Think “end the syllable on L,” and only pronounce the “T” if the next syllable begins with a vowel; otherwise, expect the next consonant to sound extra “tight/tense.”

It’s like the sound in English “jeep” or “cheese,” but with little to no extra puff of air (less breathy than English “ch”), and it can sound slightly less voiced than an English “j.” Keep it light: don’t strongly aspirate it (that would be ㅊ), and don’t make it extra tense (that would be ㅉ).

Before **ㅣ** and **ㅑ ㅕ ㅛ ㅠ ㅖ ㅒ**, it shifts to a **soft “sh”** sound (close to the “sh” in “she,” with the tongue a bit closer to the teeth). Keep it unvoiced—don’t let it turn into English “z.”

thoughts: Pattern ㄱ as a final consonant (받침) is not a fully released English-style “k.” It’s a short, unreleased stop [k̚]. English speakers know the /k/ sound, but the Korean habit of cutting it off cleanly (no extra puff or vowel) takes practice. If the next syllable/word starts with a vowel, the ㄱ often links over and can sound closer to a “g” in fast, natural speech (e.g., 한국어 → 한구거).
description: At the end of a word/syllable, ㄱ is pronounced like a “k” that you stop abruptly—like saying “back” but without releasing the final k (no audible burst, no extra “uh”). Keep your tongue touching the soft palate, then stop the sound. If a vowel follows in the next syllable/word, the ㄱ may link forward and sound more like a soft “g” between vowels.

thoughts: Pattern: ㄲ. In final (batchim) position, ㄲ is not pronounced as a long/extra-strong “kk”; it neutralizes to an unreleased [k̚] (same final sound as ㄱ/ㅋ). The tricky part is what happens when something follows: before a vowel it resyllabifies and becomes tense [k͈], and before many consonants it can tense the next consonant.
description: At the end of a syllable/word, ㄲ is a cut-off, unreleased “k” sound ([k̚])—like saying the “k” in English “back” but stopping without an audible release. If the next syllable starts with a vowel (written with ㅇ), that final ㄲ usually moves over and is pronounced as a tense “kk” ([k͈])—tight, short, and with no puff of air (unlike English aspirated “k”). Before another consonant, it stays [k̚] and often makes the following consonant sound “tensed” (e.g., ㄷ→ㄸ).

thoughts: ㄴ at the end of a word is the Korean final consonant (batchim) sound [n]. It’s very close to English “n,” but Korean final consonants are held short and cleanly without adding an extra vowel. In connected speech, this ㄴ can link to the next vowel, or assimilate before certain consonants.
description: At the end of a word, ㄴ is pronounced like the English “n” in “sun,” with your tongue tip touching the ridge just behind your upper front teeth and air flowing through your nose. Keep it unreleased and crisp—don’t let an extra vowel creep in (avoid sounding like “-na/-ni”). In fast speech, final ㄴ can: (1) resyllabify before a following vowel (it sounds like it moves to the next syllable), (2) sound like [l] before ㄹ (ㄴ+ㄹ → ㄹㄹ), or (3) sound like [ŋ] before ㄱ/ㅋ/ㄲ (nasal assimilation).

thoughts: When ㄷ is written as a final consonant (받침), it doesn’t sound like a clear English “d.” It neutralizes to a short, unreleased “t” sound, and it can change/link to a “d” sound if the next syllable starts with a vowel.
description: At the end of a syllable/word, final ㄷ is pronounced as an unreleased “t” [t̚]: put your tongue in a T position, stop the air, and don’t release a puff (no audible “t” burst). If the next word/syllable begins with a vowel, the ㄷ often links over and is heard like a “d” [d] (e.g., 받+아 → 바다). Before another consonant, it stays [t̚] and may tense the next consonant (e.g., ㅂ→ㅃ).

description: When ㅆ appears at the end of a syllable/word (받침), pronounce it as a short, unreleased [t̚]—similar to the cut-off final sound in American English “cat” (no extra puff of air, and not an “s” sound). thoughts: ㄵ is a final (batchim) consonant cluster made of ㄴ+ㅈ. In most cases you only *hear* an “n” sound, but when the next syllable starts with a vowel, the ㅈ shifts over and is pronounced at the start of the next syllable. description: When ㄵ appears at the end of a syllable, it’s usually pronounced like ㄴ [n] (similar to the final **n** in English “sun,” but shorter and unreleased). If the next syllable begins with a **vowel**, the ㅈ links to the next syllable (so you get something like **n + j**): e.g., 앉아 sounds like “an-ja.” If the next syllable begins with certain **consonants**, you still pronounce [n], but the next consonant often becomes **tense** (stronger), e.g., ㄷ → ㄸ, ㅈ → ㅉ.

thoughts: ㄾ is a rare Korean final consonant cluster (받침) made of ㄹ+ㅌ. In most word-final or pre-consonant situations it’s simplified to just an ㄹ sound, but before a vowel the ㅌ is heard by linking into the next syllable. It can also tense (double) a following consonant.
description: When ㄾ appears as a final consonant (batchim), it’s usually pronounced like a final ㄹ (a light “l” sound), with the ㅌ not clearly released. If the next syllable starts with a vowel, the ㅌ “moves over” and is pronounced as a clear [t] at the start of the next syllable (…ㄾ+아/어 → …l-ta/teo). If the next syllable starts with a consonant (like ㄷ), the hidden ㅌ often makes that consonant tense (e.g., ㄷ → ㄸ), so you hear something like “…l-tta” rather than an extra “t” sound.

thoughts: ㅀ is a final consonant cluster (batchim) made of ㄹ+ㅎ. In actual speech the ㅎ is usually not heard as a separate sound, but it often changes the next sound (especially by making it aspirated). English speakers know an “L” sound, but the rule-based alternations (silent ㅎ + aspiration/linking) are new.
description: When ㅀ appears as a final consonant: (1) At the end of a word or before most consonants, it’s usually just an L sound [l] (the ㅎ is silent). (2) Before a vowel, the ㅎ drops and the ㄹ links to the next syllable, so it sounds like a plain ㄹ starting the next syllable (e.g., …-러). (3) Before ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ, the ㅎ “aspirates” the next consonant: ㄱ→ㅋ, ㄷ→ㅌ, ㅂ→ㅍ, ㅈ→ㅊ (so you get a stronger puff of air). (4) Before ㄴ, the ㄴ often turns into ㄹ, giving a doubled L sound (…-ll-).

thoughts: ㄿ is a rare final consonant cluster. When it’s followed by ㅇ (i.e., the next syllable starts with a vowel), Korean usually splits it across the syllables: ㄹ stays as a final -l sound, and ㅍ moves to the next syllable as an aspirated p.

thoughts: ㅄ is a complex final consonant (batchim). thoughts: ㄹㅎ is a 받침 (final-consonant) cluster. In most cases you mainly hear the ㄹ sound, while ㅎ either disappears or affects the *next* consonant by making it aspirated.
description:
How it sounds depends on what comes next:
- **Before a pause or another consonant:** it’s basically just **ㄹ = [l]** (like the “l” in *fall*). The **ㅎ is usually not heard**.
- **Before a vowel (linking to the next syllable):** the **ㅎ drops**, and the ㄹ often links over and sounds like the Korean in-between **ㄹ = [ɾ]** (a quick tap, similar to the American English flapped “t” in *butter*).
- **Before a plain consonant ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ:** the **ㅎ makes the next consonant aspirated**: ㄱ→ㅋ, ㄷ→ㅌ, ㅂ→ㅍ, ㅈ→ㅊ (you still keep the ㄹ sound before it).

description:

2) When a vowel follows (값이) or when ㅂ is the coda and ㅅ starts the next syllable (밥상, 입술): the ㅅ sound comes out, and it’s commonly tensed to “ss” (a tighter, sharper s). So it can sound like “p + ss…”.

thoughts: ㄱㅅ shows up either as (1) a syllable-final consonant cluster ㄳ (usually sounds like just a final ㄱ), or (2) across a syllable boundary where a final ㄱ is followed by an initial ㅅ (often making the ㅅ sound tense like ㅆ). English speakers know “k” and “s,” but the Korean unreleased final ㄱ and the automatic tensing of ㅅ can feel new.
description:
Main pronunciations:
- As the complex final consonant ㄳ (batchim): usually pronounce only the ㄱ as an unreleased [k̚] (like the “k” in ‘back’ but without a puff/release). The ㅅ is not heard.
- If that ㄳ is followed by a vowel, the ㅅ typically carries over to the next syllable and is pronounced as a tense ㅆ sound (a tighter, sharper ‘s’): ㄳ+V → [k̚][s͈V].
- If ㄱ is a final consonant and the next syllable starts with ㅅ (…ㄱㅅ… in spelling), that ㅅ commonly becomes tense ㅆ: …ㄱ+ㅅ… → …[k̚][s͈]…
Tip: keep the ㄱ “closed” (no released k), then start a very crisp ‘ss’ for the ㅅ/ㅆ.

thoughts: The written sequence ㄱㄷ typically occurs across a syllable boundary: a final ㄱ (batchim) followed by an initial ㄷ. In standard pronunciation, the ㄱ is an unreleased [k̚] and the following ㄷ is commonly tensified to ㄸ [t͈], so it often sounds like “k-tt” rather than a clearly released “k-t.”
description: When ㄱ is the final consonant of a syllable and the next syllable begins with ㄷ, the ㄱ is pronounced as a short, unreleased “k” (like the cut-off k in English “book” said quickly), and the ㄷ usually becomes tense ㄸ (a tight, hard “tt” with no puff of air). So ㄱㄷ is often heard as [k̚t͈] (e.g., 맥도… → 맥또…). Tip: stop the “k” abruptly (don’t release it), then say a firm “tt” (not aspirated like English “top”).

description: When ㄱ is the end consonant (batchim) and the next syllable starts with ㅂ, the ㄱ is a short, unreleased “k” sound (like the stop at the end of English “buc(k)”), and the following ㅂ is typically *tensed* to ㅃ, sounding like a tight, strong “pp” (not an English “b”). So ㄱㅂ is usually pronounced close to [k̚p͈], e.g., 국밥 ≈ “guk-ppap.” In very careful/slow speech you may hear it less tensed, but the “pp” pronunciation is common and natural.

thoughts: ㄷㅂ is a letter sequence that usually spans two syllables (…ㄷ + ㅂ…). The sound changes mainly depending on whether ㄷ is a syllable-final 받침 (often triggering a tensing of the following ㅂ) or a syllable-initial consonant (just a normal ㄷ sound before ㅂ).
description:
Two common pronunciations:
1) If ㄷ is syllable-final (받침) and the next syllable starts with ㅂ, ㄷ is an unreleased [t̚] (like a cut-off “t”), and the following ㅂ is usually pronounced tense, closer to “pp” ([p͈]). To English ears it can sound like “t-pp”.
2) If ㄷ is syllable-initial (not 받침), it’s the Korean plain ㄷ (between English t/d depending on position), followed by the plain ㅂ (between p/b). No special tensing is forced just because ㄷ is before ㅂ across syllables.
Tip: For case (1), stop the tongue for ㄷ without releasing a puff of air, then start the next ㅂ with a tighter, firmer closure (like a very crisp ‘p’).

description:
In regular words, when **ㅅ is a final consonant (받침)** it’s pronounced like a short, unreleased **t** (not an ‘s’). If the next syllable starts with **ㅂ**, that ㅂ commonly becomes **tense ㅃ**, so **ㅅㅂ** is often heard like **“t-pp”** (e.g., 맛보다 ≈ “mat-ppoda”).

Separately, **ㅅㅂ** is also widely used online as a **consonant-only abbreviation** for **시발** (a strong swear; roughly “f***”), usually read as **“시발”** (sounds like “shee-bal”), or sometimes spelled by letter names (“시옷 비읍”).
